1.q: בֶּן־עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְ⁠אַחַ֤ת שָׁנָה֙ צִדְקִיָּ֣הוּ בְ⁠מָלְכ֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠אַחַ֤ת עֶשְׂרֵה֙ שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּ⁠ירֽוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְ⁠שֵׁ֣ם אִמּ֔⁠וֹ חמיטל בַּֽת־יִרְמְיָ֖הוּ מִ⁠לִּבְנָֽה
1.note: In this verse and the next verse, the author is introducing **Zedekiah** as a participant in the story as the new king of **Judah**. To translate this verse, if you have already translated the book of 2 Kings, see how you translated the same material in 2 Kings 24:18–19.

2.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 18:4. Alternate translation: [And he did what Yahweh considered to be evil]

3.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:35. Alternate translation: [the anger of Yahweh]

The author is using **it was against** as a common expression of his culture to mean “it happened to.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [this came upon Jerusalem and Judah] or [this happened to Jerusalem and Judah]

Here, the **face** of Yahweh represents his presence, and in this context it means specifically the land of Israel, where Yahweh was understood to be present in a special way. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [away from the land of Israel]

4.note: The author is using this phrase to introduce a new event. See how you translated it in 13:6.

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **ninth** or **tenth**, you could represent these numbers in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in year nine of his reign, in month ten]
The pronoun **his** refers to Zedekiah, not to Nebuchadnezzar. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [of Zedekiah’s reign]

The author is using the adjective **ten** as a noun to mean a certain day. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [on day ten of the month] or [on the tenth day of the month]
The pronoun **they** refers to Nebuchadnezzar’s **army**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and his army built] or [and his soldiers built]

5.note: The author is using **entered into siege** as a common expression of his culture to mean that the Nebuchadnezzar’s soldiers besieged the city. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the city came under siege] or [And they besieged the city]
If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **eleventh**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [year 11]

6.note: The author is using the adjective **nine** as a noun to mean a certain day. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [on day nine of the month] or [on the ninth day of the month]

The author is speaking of **famine** as if it were a living thing that could have **seized the city**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [there was serious famine throughout the city]
See how you translated the term “bread’ in 38:9. Alternate translation: [food]

7.note: The expression **was breached** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the Chaldeans breached the city] or [And the Babylonians breached the city]

The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

Recall what you decided in 21:4 about whether to use the name **Chaldeans** when it is in the original text or to use the name “Babylonians” throughout the book. Alternate translation: [now the Babylonians]

As the next verse indicates, King Zedekiah **fled** along with the **men of war** (his soldiers). You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and King Zedekiah and all of the men of war fled]

8.note: The expression **were scattered** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [scattered]

9.note: See how you translated the expression “Go up” in 22:20. Alternate translation: [and they brought him]

Here the author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. (The context suggests that Nebuchadnezzar specifically may have **pronounced judgment** on Zedekiah. The UST reflects this interpretation.) Alternate translation: [And judgment was pronounced on him]

10.note: The author is using one person who was involved in the action he describes, **the king of Babylon**, to mean everyone who was involved. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the king of Babylon ordered his soldiers to slaughter … and he also ordered them to slaughter]
Here, **eyes** represent “sight.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in his sight]

11.note: The author is using one person who was involved in these actions, **the king of Babylon**, who commanded his soldiers to do them, to mean everyone who was involved. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use plural pronouns, which would refer back to Nebuchadnezzar’s soldiers. Alternate translation: [they blinded … and they bound him … and they brought him]

The is using the possessive form to describe a **house** or building that was characterized by being a place of **oversight**, that is, a place where people were watched carefully. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation, as in the UST: [in prison]

12.note: If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **fifth**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [And in month five]

The author is using the adjective **seven** as a noun to mean a certain day. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [on day seven of the month] or [on the seventh day of the month]

12.q: הִ֗יא שְׁנַת֙ תְּשַֽׁע־עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה שָׁנָ֔ה לַ⁠מֶּ֖לֶךְ נְבוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֣ר
12.note: If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **the year of 19**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [it was the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar]

Here, **he stood to the face** (that is, he stood in the presence) represents how **Nebuzaradan** was an important official of the **king of Babylon**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. The UST models one way to do that.

13.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 7:2. Alternate translation: [the temple of Yahweh]

The author is saying **all the houses of Jerusalem** as an overstatement for emphasis. The phrase **every house of the great** limits the meaning of that phrase. Alternate translation: [And all of the houses of Jerusalem, that is, every house of the great]

The author is using the adjective **great** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [every house that belonged to a great person] or [every great house]
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:10. Alternate translation: [he burned down]

15.note: The expression **left** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [remaining]

See how you translated the similar expression in 38:19. Alternate translation: [and the ones having gone over, who had gone over to the king of Babylon] or [and the ones having deserted, who had deserted to the king of Babylon]

It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [and the ones who had deserted to the king of Babylon]

By **the multitude**, the author probably means the people of Judah who lived in places other than Jerusalem. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the rest of the Judeans who lived in places other than Jerusalem]

16.note: The author is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [But Nebuzaradan, the chief of the guards, let some of the poor people who lived in the land remain]

17.q: וְ⁠אֶת־עַמּוּדֵ֨י הַ⁠נְּחֹ֜שֶׁת אֲשֶׁ֣ר לְ⁠בֵית־יְהוָ֗ה וְֽ⁠אֶת־הַ⁠מְּכֹנ֞וֹת וְ⁠אֶת־יָ֧ם הַ⁠נְּחֹ֛שֶׁת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בְּ⁠בֵית־יְהוָ֖ה שִׁבְּר֣וּ כַשְׂדִּ֑ים
17.note: It might seem that repeating the information that these things were in **the house of Yahweh** would be to express extra information in a way that would not be natural in your language. If so, you can provide the information only once. Alternate translation: [And the Chaldeans broke up the pillars of bronze and the stands and the sea of bronze that were at the house of Yahweh]

18.note: The author is using the term **palms** to mean some implement that the priests used in the temple area that had a cupped shape. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Kings 7:50. This could mean: (1) Alternate translation: [incense dishes] or (2) Alternate translation: [spoons] or [ladles]

The pronoun **they** refers to the priests who **served** at the temple. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the priests served] or [the priests did their work]

19.note: The author is repeating the words **gold** and **silver** in order to indicate that these articles were made of pure gold and pure silver. The description of them in 1 Kings 7:50 says that plainly, and you could do the same here in your translation. Alternate translation: [that were pure gold and that were pure silver]

21.note: The author is saying **four fingers** as a unit of measurement. It is equivalent to a “handbreadth,” which the biblical author uses in 1 Kings 7:26 for the thickness of the bronze sea. This distance corresponded to the width of a man’s hand measured across the palm, or about eight centimeters or about three and a half inches. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this width in modern measurements, either in the text of your translation or in a footnote.

22.note: The demonstrative pronoun **these** refers not just to the **pomegranates** but to all of the dimensions and features of the first pillar. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the second pillar had the same dimensions and features]
If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **second**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [to the other pillar]

23.note: The author is using **to the wind** as a common expression of his culture to mean “in each direction that the wind blows,” in other words, facing the four main directions of north, east, south, and west. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And a total of 96 pomegranates were on the four sides of each pillar]

24.note: The author is using the term **head** to mean “chief” or “leading.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the high priest]

25.note: The author is using the phrase **seers of the face of the king** to describe royal advisors, since they regularly spoke with the king in person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [seven royal advisors]

25.q: אֲשֶׁ֣ר נִמְצְא֣וּ בָ⁠עִ֔יר & הַֽ⁠נִּמְצְאִ֖ים בְּ⁠ת֥וֹךְ הָ⁠עִֽיר
25.note: The author is using the term **found** in a way characteristic of his language and culture to mean that these **men** could be found, that is, they were present in the **city**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who were in the city … who were in the midst of the city]

27.note: The verbs **struck** and **killed** together express a single idea. The verb **struck** tells in what way the king of Babylon **killed** these men. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [And the king of Babylon violently killed the] or [And the king of Babylon executed them]

It is unlikely that **the king of Babylon** did this personally. The author is likely using the king, who ordered this, to represent everyone who was involved, including the soldiers who carried out his order. Alternate translation: [the king of Babylon ordered his soldiers to execute them]

28.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 52:12. Alternate translation: [In the seventh year of his reign]

29.note: See how you translated the similar expression in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [In the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign]

Here the word **soul** is singular in form, but it refers to all of the souls whom Nebuchadnezzar exiled. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “soul.” Alternate translation: [souls]

The author is using one part of these people, their souls, to mean all of them in the act of being taken into exile. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people]

30.note: See how you translated the similar expressions in the previous two verses. Alternate translation: [In the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign]

30.q: יְהוּדִ֕ים נֶ֕פֶשׁ שְׁבַ֥ע מֵא֖וֹת אַרְבָּעִ֣ים וַ⁠חֲמִשָּׁ֑ה כָּל־נֶ֕פֶשׁ אַרְבַּ֥עַת אֲלָפִ֖ים וְ⁠שֵׁ֥שׁ מֵאֽוֹת
30.note: See how you translated the term “soul” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [745 Judean people. The total number of people was 4,600]

31.note: The author is using this phrase to introduce a new event. See how you translated it in [2:1](ta:02).

31.q: בִ⁠שְׁלֹשִׁ֨ים וָ⁠שֶׁ֜בַע שָׁנָ֗ה לְ⁠גָלוּת֙ יְהוֹיָכִ֣ן מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֔ה בִּ⁠שְׁנֵ֤ים עָשָׂר֙ חֹ֔דֶשׁ בְּ⁠עֶשְׂרִ֥ים וַ⁠חֲמִשָּׁ֖ה לַ⁠חֹ֑דֶשׁ
31.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 52:12. Alternate translation: [in the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin, the king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-fifth day of the month]

The author is using **lifted the head** as a common expression of his culture to mean that Evil Merodach brought Jehoiachin from a lower position to a higher position. Alternate translation: [improved the situation of Jehoiachin]

32.note: The author is using the adjective **good**, which is plural, as a noun to mean things of a certain kind. The ULT shows that by supplying the word **things**. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent word or phrase. Alternate translation: [kindly]

The author may not mean that Jehoiachin’s seat was **above** or physically higher than that of other kings. He may be saying **above** to mean “more honorable.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he gave him a more honored place than the kings]

In this verse, the word **seat** is singular in form, but it refers to the seats of all of these **kings**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “text.” Alternate translation: [above the seats of the kings]

33.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Evil Merodach, while the pronoun **his** refers to Jehoiachin. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Evil Merodach changed the clothes of Jehoiachin’s imprisonment] or [And Evil Merodach allowed Jehoiachin to wear the clothes of a courtier rather than those of a prisoner]

Giving Jehoiachin different clothes to wear was a symbolic action by which Evil Merodach showed that Jehoiachin’s status had changed from prisoner to honored guest. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And he changed the clothes of his imprisonment to show that he was no longer a prisoner]

The pronoun **he** refers to Jehoiachin, while the pronoun **his** refers to Evil Merodach. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Jehoiachin ate bread regularly to the face of Evil Merodach]
See how you translated the similar expression in 52:6. Alternate translation: [meals]

Here, the **face** of Evil Merodach represents his “presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in his presence]

The author is using the term **days** to refer to a specific time, the lifetime of Jehoiachin. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [throughout his lifetime]

34.q: וַ⁠אֲרֻחָת֗⁠וֹ אֲרֻחַת֩ תָּמִ֨יד נִתְּנָה־לּ֜⁠וֹ מֵ⁠אֵ֧ת מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֛ל
34.note: It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [And a continual allowance was given to him from the king of Babylon]

34.q: וַ⁠אֲרֻחָת֗⁠וֹ אֲרֻחַת֩ תָּמִ֨יד נִתְּנָה־לּ֜⁠וֹ מֵ⁠אֵ֧ת מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֛ל
34.note: The expression **was given** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the king gave him a continual allowance]

The author is using **the matter of a day in its day** as a common expression of his culture to mean “at a fixed daily rate.” (He does not necessarily mean that the **allowance** was paid out each day, but that it was calculated at a daily rate.) If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of Nehemiah, see how you translated the same expression in Nehemiah 11:23. Alternate translation: [at a fixed daily rate]

The phrases **until the day of his death** and **all of the days of his life** mean similar things. The author is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [throughout the rest of his lifetime]
